title: Active Directory Trusts: Authentication Paths Are Security Boundaries
summary: Understand intra-forest trust behavior, external trust purpose, and why trust design must be treated as an identity-security decision rather than simple connectivity.
objective: Explain trust direction and transitivity, identify the authentication boundary being crossed, and require explicit security review before creating or broadening a trust.
body_outline: Domains inside one forest are linked by automatic two-way transitive trust relationships; external trusts extend authentication to domains outside that forest.
A trust allows authentication to cross a directory boundary but does not by itself grant access to every resource; authorization still depends on permissions and group membership.
Trust design expands the set of identities that may be evaluated for access, so ownership, lifecycle, authentication scope and monitoring must be documented before implementation.
Troubleshoot trust failures by separating name resolution, network reachability, secure-channel/authentication, and authorization rather than recreating the trust as a first response.
quick_check: Why is creating a trust a security-architecture change even if no file permissions are changed at the same time?

title: AD Trusts in Plain English: Who Will Accept Whose Identity?
summary: A trust tells one directory when it may rely on authentication performed by another directory; it does not automatically grant access to every resource.
analogy: A trust is like one company agreeing to accept another company's employee badge as valid identity proof. The badge still does not open every door; each door keeps its own access list.
plain_language_explanation: Trusts extend authentication paths between domains or forests. Resource permissions remain separate, so engineers must reason about both authentication and authorization when diagnosing or designing cross-domain access.
visual_hint: Two forests connected by a trust arrow, with a separate ACL gate protecting the target resource.
quick_check: Does a trust automatically give every user in the trusted domain access to every server in the trusting domain?

title: Privileged Access Architecture: Tier 0, Secure Admin Hosts and Authentication Silos
summary: Apply identity-tiering principles so compromise of a lower-trust endpoint does not expose credentials that control Active Directory or other higher-tier systems.
architecture_notes: The AD DS tier model separates Tier 0 identity-control assets from Tier 1 servers/applications and Tier 2 end-user devices. Administrative identities and workstations should not cross downward into lower-trust tiers in ways that expose reusable privileged credentials.
internals: Authentication policy silos can contain selected user, computer and service accounts and restrict where those credentials may be used. This complements OU delegation and privileged-access workstation design; it is not a substitute for least privilege or clean administrative boundaries.
failure_modes: Common failures include using Domain Admin credentials on ordinary workstations, allowing service accounts to authenticate broadly, permanently assigning high privilege, and administering Tier 0 assets from compromised or unmanaged endpoints.
trade_offs: Stronger tier separation and authentication restrictions reduce credential theft paths but increase operational discipline, dedicated administrative-device requirements and exception-management overhead.
enterprise_design_notes: Treat Tier 0 as the identity control plane: domain controllers, privileged directory groups and any system capable of controlling them require the strongest credential, workstation, monitoring and change controls.

title: Read-only Trust and Cross-Domain Access Evidence Collection
summary: Collect trust, DNS and authentication evidence without modifying trust configuration or privileged group membership.
objective: Determine whether a cross-domain access failure is caused by trust-path, DNS/DC discovery or resource authorization before any trust change is attempted.
prerequisites_detail: Controlled lab or approved troubleshooting context with two domains/forests and read access to directory/trust information.
environment: Two trusted AD domains or forests plus one target resource with known permissions.
topology: Client identity domain -> trust path -> target domain/forest -> resource ACL.
steps: Record the source identity domain, target resource domain and expected trust direction.
Verify DNS resolution and DC discovery for both directory namespaces.
Query the existing trust configuration with approved read-only administrative tools and record direction/transitivity.
Test authentication separately from authorization by confirming the user can obtain identity validation while still checking the target resource ACL independently.
Document the first failing boundary and escalate with evidence instead of deleting or recreating the trust.
expected_result: The engineer can state whether the failure is DNS/DC discovery, trust/authentication, or target-resource authorization without making configuration changes.
validation: Cross-check the observed trust direction against documented architecture and repeat from the opposite side only if the scenario requires bidirectional access.
rollback: Not required; the exercise is read-only.
cleanup: Remove diagnostic exports containing internal domain names according to lab or incident-data handling policy.

title: Cross-Domain Authentication Fails: Trust, DNS or Authorization?
summary: A bounded decision tree for cross-domain incidents that prevents destructive trust recreation before the failing layer is identified.
symptoms: Users from another domain cannot authenticate to a resource
Authentication succeeds but access is denied
Trust-related errors appear after DNS or network changes
diagnostic_order: Confirm source and target domains and intended trust direction.
Validate DNS resolution and DC location for both namespaces.
Confirm the configured trust exists and matches the documented topology.
Separate authentication failure from authorization failure by checking the target ACL and effective group membership.
Escalate secure-channel or trust-repair actions only after the failing layer is evidenced.
escalation_boundary: Do not delete, recreate or broaden a production trust as a diagnostic shortcut. Trust mutation requires explicit change approval and rollback planning.

title: Domain Controller Hardening and Windows Server 2025 Identity Security Defaults
summary: Protect domain controllers as Tier 0 assets and understand security-default changes that can expose legacy compatibility dependencies during Windows Server 2025 adoption.
objective: Prioritize Tier 0 hardening controls and identify Windows Server 2025 protocol-security changes that require compatibility testing before broad deployment.
body_outline: Domain controllers are identity-control-plane assets; Microsoft recommends least privilege, secure administrative hosts, patching, application control and reduction of unnecessary attack surface.
Administrative credentials used for Tier 0 must not be exposed on ordinary user endpoints or lower-trust server tiers.
Windows Server 2025 requires inbound and outbound SMB signing by default, strengthening integrity and relay resistance compared with older defaults.

Protocol hardening can expose legacy clients, appliances and workflows. Inventory, monitoring, staged testing and rollback criteria are required before weakening a new default or enforcing an equivalent control in an older estate.
quick_check: Why is disabling a new Windows Server 2025 signing requirement to restore legacy compatibility a security exception rather than a routine fix?

title: AD Trust, Tier 0 and Domain Controller Security Checkpoint
summary: Scenario assessment covering trust boundaries, privileged-access tiering, authentication silos and Windows Server 2025 protocol-security defaults.

assessment_items.question: A user from a trusted forest authenticates successfully but gets Access Denied on one share. Should the trust be rebuilt first?
assessment_items.answer: No. Authentication crossed the trust successfully; investigate resource authorization, effective group membership and the target ACL first.

assessment_items.question: Why should a Domain Admin avoid signing in to a normal user workstation?
assessment_items.answer: A compromised lower-trust workstation can capture or reuse privileged credentials and create a path into the Tier 0 identity control plane.

assessment_items.question: What problem can an authentication policy silo help reduce?
assessment_items.answer: It can restrict selected high-privilege user, computer or service credentials to designated systems, reducing where those credentials can be used or exposed.

assessment_items.question: A legacy appliance breaks when Windows Server 2025 SMB signing is required. What is the correct engineering response?
assessment_items.answer: Treat it as a compatibility/security exception: identify the dependency, test remediation or replacement, assess risk and use approved rollback/exception governance rather than casually weakening the default.

title: Senior AD Engineer Interview: Trust Boundaries, Tier 0 and Hardening Trade-offs
summary: Senior scenarios testing judgement across cross-forest authentication, credential-tiering and Windows Server 2025 hardening changes.

questions.question: How do you troubleshoot a cross-forest access failure without immediately modifying the trust?
answer_points: map trust direction and intended access
capture exact errors and effective access
change trust configuration only with evidence and approval

questions.question: How would you reduce the risk of privileged AD credentials being stolen from lower-tier systems?
answer_points: restrict where high-value accounts can authenticate

questions.question: What do Windows Server 2025 stronger signing defaults change for an upgrade programme?
answer_points: improve protocol integrity and relay resistance
security exceptions need explicit risk ownership
do not weaken defaults without evidence and rollback governance
